A rule for stepping out before a crash: 65 years of a moving-average exit on the S&P/TSX

A simple, mechanical way to act on the fear of a crash is to sell when the index closes below its average of recent months and buy back when it rises above it. Using Statistics Canada’s monthly S&P/TSX Composite closes and treasury bill yields from 1958 to 2023, see what such a rule avoided, what it cost in false alarms, how much depended on assumptions, and why the account it runs in matters.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

From 1958-01 to 2023-09, in a TFSA, so no tax, $10,000 that stayed in a fund following the S&P/TSX Composite price plus a 2.5% yield less a 0.5% fee became $1,608,633 (8.04% a year); switching to treasury bills whenever the month-end close fell below its 10-month average became $2,242,662 (8.59% a year), with 58 exits to cash, 40 of them bought back at a higher index level. Its deepest fall was -24.7% against -43.9%. Across 669 rolling 10-year periods the rule ended ahead in 72.5%. Prices rose 957% over the whole test. Dated index and yield history with assumed dividends, fees, costs and taxes; not a forecast or a recommendation.

The central idea

Applied to the S&P/TSX Composite from January 1958 to September 2023 with an assumed 2.5% dividend yield, a 0.5% fee and a 0.1% cost per switch, a rule that held treasury bills whenever the month-end close was below its 10-month average cut the deepest fall from 44% to 25% and, inside a TFSA, ended ahead (8.6% a year against 8.0%). But 40 of its 58 exits were bought back at a higher index level, it was in cash a third of the time, almost all of its lead came before 2009 and it fell behind from there, and its edge disappeared with a 4% dividend yield or in a taxable account. A 24-month version of the same idea lost badly. The rule changes the kind of risk you carry; it does not remove it.

01

Turning fear of a crash into a rule

Most people who worry about a 2008-style crash do not want to predict one. They want a way out that does not depend on their nerves on a bad day. The simplest mechanical version is a moving-average rule: at each month-end, compare the index with the average of its last ten closes. If it is below, sell the fund and hold treasury bills; if it is back above, buy the fund again. No forecasts, no headlines.

Rules like this are often shown with impressive backtests. This guide runs one on Statistics Canada’s monthly S&P/TSX Composite closes, January 1958 to September 2023, with the 3-month treasury bill yield for the months in cash, and then changes the assumptions that backtests usually hold still: the dividend yield, trading costs, the length of the average, the starting date and, above all, tax. The account starts in January 1958 so that even a 24-month average has two years of history behind it.

02

What the rule did over the whole period

The first chart shows the rule’s account as a share of an account that simply stayed in the same fund. With CAD 10,000, a 2.5% yield, a 0.5% fee and a 0.1% cost each time it switched, inside a TFSA, staying invested grew to about CAD 1.61 million (8.04% a year) and the 10-month rule to about CAD 2.24 million (8.59% a year). The rule held the fund in two months out of three and spent the rest in treasury bills.

The line is not a steady climb. The rule trailed for most of the 1960s, falling to 88% of the buy-and-hold account by March 1974, then gained sharply in the 1973–74 and 1981–82 bear markets, when treasury bills paid 6% to 9% and then 11% to 21% a year. It reached 2.72 times the buy-and-hold account in February 2009, after sidestepping most of the global financial crisis, and then gave back about half of that lead: by September 2023 it was at 1.39. Between 2009 and 2023, a $10,000 start would have grown to about CAD 30,100 staying invested and CAD 16,500 under the rule. The best-and-worst-months guide explains why the gains from avoiding falls and the losses from missing rebounds tend to arrive close together.

03

Smaller falls, but not no falls

What the rule did reliably was shorten the worst falls. The second chart tracks each account against its own previous high. Staying invested, the deepest fall was 44%, at the bottom in February 2009; the rule’s deepest was 25%. From June 2008 to February 2009 staying invested lost 43% and the rule 5%, because the index closed below its average in July 2008. From August 2000 to September 2002 the figures were −43% and −15%; from October 1973 to September 1974, −35% and −7%.

The rule’s own worst fall shows its blind spot. In October 1987 the index fell about 23% within a single month, before any month-end signal could react, so the rule took the whole fall, sold at the October close and bought back in June 1988 at a higher level. In 2020 it sold at the end of February, avoided most of March, and bought back in July at about the level it had sold. A month-end rule only reacts after the index has already fallen through its average, and it cannot help at all with a crash that happens between two month-ends.

04

The price of the false alarms

The third chart counts exits by decade and how many of them were bought back at a higher index level than the sale. Over the whole period the 10-month rule sold 58 times; 40 of those exits ended with the fund repurchased higher, so each of those round trips lost ground before costs and tax, cushioned only by the interest earned while out. Many lasted one or two months: in 2015 alone it sold in March and June and bought back in April and in 2016. Only a handful of exits, such as 1974, 1981, 2000, 2002 and 2008, caught most of a deep fall.

This is the trade a timing rule makes: frequent small losses in exchange for occasional large avoided losses. Whether it pays depends on how often deep falls happen in the years you happen to hold it, which nobody knows in advance. A 2% buffer, which sells only when the close is 2% below the average and buys only when it is 2% above, cut the exits to 31 and the losing round trips to 18 in this history. The false-alarm guide works out how often a crash warning has to be right to pay for itself.

05

How much of the result came from assumptions

The fourth chart reruns the comparison for every starting month and several holding periods, for averages from 3 to 24 months. With the defaults, the 10-month rule ended ahead in 72% of rolling ten-year periods. But nearby choices tell a different story: a 24-month average ended ahead in only 10% of ten-year periods and turned CAD 10,000 into about CAD 267,000 over the full span, a sixth of staying invested. Starting from 2009, the 10-month rule was behind in every ten-year period available.

The dividend yield matters too. The index in this data is a price index, so dividends are added as an assumed constant. Raise it from 2.5% to 4%, closer to what Canadian stocks often paid before 2000, and staying invested grows to about CAD 4.28 million while the rule reaches CAD 4.29 million: the gap all but vanishes, because the rule gives up a third of the dividends while it sits in cash. A rule chosen after seeing which length worked best in the past will usually look better in that past than it does afterwards.

06

The account decides whether trading is cheap

Inside a TFSA, the Canada Revenue Agency says investment income, including capital gains, is generally tax-free even when withdrawn, so selling and buying back costs only the trading expense. In a taxable account every exit at a gain is a sale. CRA’s capital gains guide sets the inclusion rate at one-half, so half of each net gain is taxed at your marginal rate in the year of the sale, and interest earned while in treasury bills is taxed in full. Staying invested defers the tax on the gain until the units are finally sold or deemed sold.

Set a 45% tax rate on interest and gains and 25% on dividends, and over the full period staying invested ends at about CAD 907,000 after selling everything at the end, while the rule ends at about CAD 508,000: from ahead by 39% inside a TFSA to behind by 44% in a taxable account, with the same trades. Losing round trips also run into the superficial loss rule: CRA disallows a loss when the same property is bought back within 30 calendar days after the sale, as a sale at one month-end and repurchase at the next can be. The fund itself carries no tax exemption; the account’s rules decide what each switch costs. The exit-tax guide works out how far a taxable fund has to fall before a sale pays for its tax.

07

A different way to carry less crash risk

The rule’s real result is a different shape of risk: fewer deep falls, more frequent small regrets, a third of the time in cash, and an outcome that hinges on settings chosen in advance. Someone who expects to abandon a rule after three false alarms in a row would have got neither its protection nor buy-and-hold’s gains.

A fixed mix, such as a balanced fund that holds bonds beside stocks and rebalances, lowers the depth of falls without trying to time them, and keeps the decision away from the worst days. It has its own costs: lower long-run growth and the occasional year, like 2022, when stocks and bonds fall together. The balanced fund guide and the rebalancing guide work through that alternative, and the keep-or-pause guide covers the separate question of new contributions from pay during a fall.

08

What this history can and cannot tell you

  • The S&P/TSX series is a price index that leaves out dividends; the constant yield you choose stands in for them. Treasury bill yields are auction averages, not what a savings account or money-market fund paid after its fees.
  • Trades happen at month-end closes with no delay; real orders take time and the fund’s price can differ from the index.
  • Taxes are simplified: dividends and interest are taxed as they arrive at your rates, net capital losses are carried forward, and the superficial loss rule is not applied.
  • Starting months overlap heavily, so the rolling shares rest on far fewer independent periods than the counts suggest.
  • The series covers one market and ends in September 2023. The same rule can behave very differently in another market or another era.
  • Nothing here predicts future returns or recommends buying, selling or holding any investment.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. Every chart applies the actual monthly price changes of the S&P/TSX Composite Index from Statistics Canada table 10-10-0125-01 (vector v122620, January 1956 to September 2023) and the 3-month treasury bill auction average yield from table 10-10-0122-01 (vector v122541) for the same months, both retrieved through the Web Data Service on 27 October 2026. The dividend yield, fund fee, trading cost, tax rates and starting amount are your assumptions and are held constant; they are not history. Nothing here forecasts the index, interest rates or any fund. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  2. Statistics Canada · Financial market statistics, last Wednesday unless otherwise stated, Bank of Canada (table 10-10-0122-01) ↗

    Treasury bill auction, average yields: 3 month, vector v122541, monthly, complete for January 1956 to September 2023 (0.06% to 20.82% in that span); latest release 9 October 2026 with September 2026 at 2.387%. Retrieved through the Web Data Service on 27 October 2026; SHA-256 of the download c04f75be…bf359f2ed, kept locally and not republished.

  3. Statistics Canada · Consumer Price Index, monthly, not seasonally adjusted (table 18-10-0004-01) ↗

    All-items CPI, vector v41690973, used only to state how much prices rose over the period tested (January 1958 to September 2023: about tenfold).

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · Guide T4037, Capital Gains – 2025 ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026: the inclusion rate is generally 1/2; a superficial loss arises when the same or identical property is bought within 30 calendar days before or after the sale and still held 30 days after it.

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · Capital losses and deductions ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026: the inclusion rate for 2025 is 50%; net capital losses can reduce taxable capital gains of the three previous years or any future year; a superficial loss is not allowed but is usually added to the cost base of the substituted property.

  6. Canada Revenue Agency · What is a TFSA ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026: income earned in a TFSA, including capital gains, is generally tax-free, even when withdrawn.
